title: Why Do Fewer Renters Expect to Move? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: New York Fed SCE Housing Survey data show renters' mean three-year moving probability fell from roughly 57 percent in 2014 to about 37 percent in 2026, tracking a slide in the average self-assessed chance of ever owning a home from ~52 percent (2015) to ~35 percent (2025). The authors attribute this to perceived mortgage affordability — the share calling a mortgage very difficult to obtain rose from ~27 percent (2021) to over 45 percent (2024) and expected rates more than doubled to ~6.8 percent — while the desire to own stayed flat at 65-74 percent, implying deferred rather than destroyed first-time-buyer demand.

insights.claim: U.S. renters' mean self-reported probability of moving within three years fell from roughly 57 percent in 2014 to about 37 percent in 2026, a 20-percentage-point drop, per the New York Fed SCE Housing Survey.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
entities: New York Fed SCE Housing Survey
insights.so_what: A 20pp collapse in intended renter turnover is a direct headwind to moving-linked consumption (movers, furniture, appliances, brokerage) and a tailwind to apartment-REIT renewal rates.
insights.locator: Renters' Expected 3-Year Mobility Fell 20 Percentage Points in the Last 12 Years

insights.claim: Homeowners' expected three-year moving probability fell from about 21 percent to 14 percent between 2014 and 2026, a smaller relative decline than renters experienced over the same period.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Owners get all the mortgage-lock-in headlines, but renters are the faster-deteriorating leg of U.S. household mobility — watch renter turnover data, not just existing-home sales.
insights.quote: Relative to their initial levels, expected mobility declined somewhat more for renters than for homeowners.
insights.locator: Renters' Expected 3-Year Mobility Fell 20 Percentage Points

insights.claim: Because renters are not subject to mortgage rate lock-in yet still show a larger relative decline in expected mobility than homeowners, mortgage lock-in cannot be the primary explanation for falling U.S. residential mobility.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Undercuts the consensus 'rates fall, lock-in unwinds, transactions normalize' trade — a rate cut releases owners but leaves the structurally frozen renter cohort largely in place.
insights.quote: renters account for roughly a third of U.S. households and, unlike homeowners, are not subject to mortgage rate lock-in
insights.locator: Americans are moving less than they used to

insights.claim: The broad U.S. decline in moving rates — from close to 20 percent annually in the mid-1980s to below 10 percent by 2019 — has persisted through business cycles and across all regions and demographic groups, marking it as structural rather than cyclical.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: A four-decade, cycle-proof halving of mobility argues against betting on a cyclical rebound in housing turnover or labor reallocation.
insights.quote: This decline has persisted through business cycles and has been evident across all regions, and has affected a broad range of demographic groups.
insights.locator: Americans are moving less than they used to

insights.claim: Expected mobility is a leading indicator: because stated moving intentions predict actual moving behavior, survey-based mobility expectations flag turns in residential mobility before transactions register them.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
entities: New York Fed SCE Housing Survey
insights.so_what: Gives an early-read overlay on housing turnover and rental churn ahead of existing-home sales and lease-turnover prints.
insights.quote: Since expected mobility predicts actual moving behavior, it provides an early signal of where residential mobility is headed before moves occur.
insights.locator: In this post, we show that the decline

insights.claim: Renters' average self-assessed probability of ever owning a home fell from roughly 52 percent in 2015 to about 35 percent by 2025, with the decline especially sharp after 2021.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: A structurally shrinking pool of expected first-time buyers is bearish for entry-level homebuilders and mortgage origination volumes, and bullish for long-duration rental demand.
insights.locator: Renters Less Optimistic About Ever Owning a Home

insights.claim: Renter moving intentions and homeownership expectations move together: renters who put only a 0–20 percent chance on ever owning report a ~25 percent three-year moving probability, versus ~76 percent for those at 81–100 percent — a gap of more than 50 percentage points.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Renter churn is effectively a proxy for first-time-buyer formation; when ownership hope dies, so does the lease turnover that drives re-leasing spreads.
insights.quote: a difference of more than 50 percentage points across the distribution.
insights.locator: Renters Who Don't Expect to Move Also Don't Expect to Ever Own a Home

insights.claim: The post frames declining renter mobility as a two-hypothesis test — affordability constraints versus a shift in preferences away from owning — and finds the evidence supports affordability, not taste.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: A reusable diagnostic: if a demand shortfall is affordability-driven it is latent and rate/price-sensitive, whereas a preference shift is permanent and un-tradeable.
insights.locator: These patterns raise a natural question

insights.claim: The share of U.S. renters who say obtaining a mortgage would be very difficult jumped from around 27 percent in 2021 to over 45 percent by 2024.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Perceived credit-box tightness, not just price, is gating first-time buyers — a signal for mortgage insurers, non-bank originators, and FHA-exposed lenders.
insights.locator: Renters Perceive Mortgages as Increasingly Difficult to Afford

insights.claim: The median mortgage rate renters believe they would receive if they applied today rose from about 3.3 percent in 2021 to nearly 6.8 percent by 2024, more than doubling in three years.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Renter rate expectations are anchored near 7 percent; a durable move below that is the trigger condition for any first-time-buyer demand release.
insights.quote: more than doubling over three years
insights.locator: Both measures suggest that mortgage access

insights.claim: Perceived ease of getting a mortgage discriminates renter mobility far more sharply than the expected rate level: mean three-year moving probability is about 66 percent for renters who say a mortgage would be very easy to get versus about 42 percent for very difficult, while moving probability slips only from about 60 percent to about 54 percent across expected rates of 3 percent to 8 percent.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Implies credit availability and qualification — not the headline rate — is the binding constraint, so easing underwriting would unlock more demand than a modest rate cut.
insights.locator: Renters Who Expect High Mortgage Rates Are Less Likely to Move

insights.claim: The share of U.S. renters who would prefer or strongly prefer to own a home if they had the financial resources has stayed in a narrow 65–74 percent band since 2015 and sat at about 65 percent in 2026, showing no collapse in the desire to own.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Demand for ownership is deferred, not destroyed — pent-up first-time-buyer demand remains a live option on any genuine affordability improvement.
insights.locator: Renters Still Prefer to Own a Home

insights.claim: Renters' view of homeownership as a good or very good investment has held in a 51 to 68 percent range since 2015, so the asset-class case for housing has not deteriorated in renters' minds even as their expectation of ever owning fell by about 17 percentage points.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Sentiment toward housing as an investment is not the marginal variable; affordability is — focus on payment-to-income and credit access metrics, not consumer housing sentiment surveys.
insights.locator: The share who view homeownership as a good or very good investment

insights.claim: Renters' growing pessimism about ever owning a home reflects affordability constraints rather than a weakening desire for homeownership, according to the New York Fed's survey evidence.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Positions falling household mobility as a fixable, policy- and rate-sensitive problem — which makes it a potential swing factor for housing-linked equities if affordability inflects.
insights.quote: reflects affordability constraints rather than a weakening desire for homeownership
insights.locator: These patterns suggest that renters' growing pessimism

insights.claim: The authors flag that their affordability-versus-mobility comparisons are unconditional — not controlling for renter credit scores or for changing economic conditions over time — so the relationship is associational rather than identified.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Discount the effect size before sizing any trade on it; the true causal contribution of affordability to mobility is likely smaller than the raw gaps imply.
insights.quote: Although these comparisons do not control for differences across renters, such as credit scores, or for changes in economic conditions over time

insights.claim: Housing affordability is presented as only one contributing factor behind declining expected renter mobility, leaving a substantial unexplained residual in the decades-long U.S. mobility slide.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Don't model the mobility decline as a pure affordability story — other structural drivers (remote work, aging, dual-earner households) remain unpriced and unmeasured here.
insights.quote: housing affordability may be one factor behind declining expected mobility among renters
